title: The white days
hookLine: three days in the middle of each lunar month

lines: A STREET LIT BY THE MOON.
A CALENDAR KEPT BY THE MOON.
THREE DAYS AT THE BRIGHT MIDDLE.
cards: On the right night of the month, the street is lit without a single lamp. The moon is full, or close to it, and the whole sky is pale.
Islam keeps its calendar by that same moon: each month begins with a thin crescent, swells to a round white face in the middle, and thins away again.
And right there, at the bright middle of every month, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ pointed his companions to three days of fasting. Not a month, like Ramadan. Not two days every week.
Three days, when the nights are at their brightest.

teach.h: ADVICE FROM A FRIEND: THREE DAYS A MONTH.

teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Hurayrah says his close friend, meaning the Prophet, advised him to keep three things: fasting three days of every month, two units of prayer in the morning, and the witr prayer before sleep.
A small, steady thing, handed to one person as friendly advice. Second, which three.

A report in the collection of al-Tirmidhi has the Prophet telling Abu Dharr that if he fasts three days of a month, let it be the thirteenth, the fourteenth and the fifteenth: the middle days of a lunar month, around the full moon.
Tradition calls them the white days, and tradition says the name comes from the nights, white with moonlight from dusk to dawn. Third, why three.

Another hadith in Bukhari, from the conversation with Abdullah ibn Amr that we'll meet tomorrow, says each good deed is counted ten times over, so fasting three days a month is like fasting all the time.
The point isn't arithmetic: something small and regular is treated as something large. Fourth, how people keep it.

teach.h: THE DATES MOVE WITH THE MOON.
teach.b: Because the dates follow the moon, the white days move against the calendar on the wall. Some Muslims check a lunar calendar each month, or an app, or the mosque's notice board, and mark the thirteenth to the fifteenth.
Some fast all three, some one or two. It's voluntary, and nobody is blamed for missing it. The white days are simply there, every month, for anyone who wants them.

how: Some Muslims fast the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of each lunar month, checking a lunar calendar or their mosque's notices to know when those days fall.

o: the nights of pilgrimage, lit by lamps across Mecca
the first three days of Ramadan, kept in white clothes
three voluntary fasts in the middle of each lunar month

p: advised: three days of every month
the bright middle of the month

s: the white days fall on the same calendar dates every year
they follow the moon, so they move against the calendar on the wall.
fasting the white days is required, like Ramadan

the white days sit at the middle of the lunar month

games.q: you're Abu Dharr. you want to fast three days a month. which three does the Prophet name?
o: the first three days of the month.
any three, as long as they're in a row.
games.why: the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth, the middle of the month, around the full moon.

practice: Picture the moon as you last saw it: thin, half, or round? You don't need the date; just ask where you'll be when it's round next, at work, at home, traveling.
If you're Muslim and you fast, you might choose one of those three days to try; if not, one of those nights simply to step outside and look up.

wordCard.voice: The white days. The thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of each lunar month, around the full moon, kept by some Muslims as three voluntary fasts. Today's word.

orig.note: 'the white days': bid is the plural of abyad, white.

carryVoice: Your line: the full-moon days. Three days at the bright middle of every month. Tomorrow: the fast of Dawud.
